## Context and objectives

:::{.highlight-last .very-small-text}
- The paper is part of EJHET special issue on methods in the history of economic thought.
- We discuss unsupervised methods and applied them to study the history of rationality in economics.

:::{.fragment .incremental}
- In this talk, we focus on the method we developed for this project;
- We build an unsupervised method that aims at:
    - exploring very large and complex corpora (10k+ articles, 1M+ sentences);
    - over long periods of time (50+ years);
    - reduce complexity to enable interpretive exploration of results; 
    - whilst taking into account the historical dimension of the data.
:::
:::

:::{.notes}
- What should the chosen method(s) be able to do:
  - handle very large corpora. Over 110 years of publications (60 million sentences and 290k economics articles).
  - Handle the historical dimension of the data. We want to be able to see how things evolve over time, and not just get a static picture or a "presentist" picture.
  - important role of textual interpretation, contextualisation, etc. Important to have a method that allows back-and-forth between quantitative results and qualitative interpretation, traditional textual analysis.
:::

:::{.notes}
- As quantitative methods are increasingly adopted in HET, what methods are used?
  - A particular type of method, quite distant from what you find in economics (no econometrics, no formal models, etc.). Less distant from quantitative sociology (MCA, PCA), but quite different when it comes to textual methods.
  - Common thread: unsupervised methods. Discovering patterns in data without presupposing what those patterns might be; identifying emergent categories.
- Bibliographic coupling.
- Topic modeling.
:::


## Unsupervised Methods 

:::{.highlight-last .very-small-text}

:::{.callout-tip .fragment .nonincremental}
### Unsupervised methods 
- Class of algorithms to identify **patterns** in unlabeled data, without predefined categories or labels as opposed to supervised methods. 
- In HET, they typically served to identify clusters of documents sharing common patterns, such as similar references (bibliographic coupling) or similar vocabulary (topic modeling).
::: 

:::{.fragment .nonincremental}
- But what do these patterns mean? Why are certain documents grouped together?
  - Requires visualisation and qualitative interpretive work to identify commonalities between observations
:::
:::

::: {.callout-important appearance ="simple" .fragment}
Qualitative and quantitative work are deeply intertwined in unsupervised methods. They are not **separate** stages, but rather a continuous back-and-forth process.
::: 


:::{.notes}
- What is the interest of unsupervised methods: avoiding anachronism, letting unexpected things emerge, enabling zoom-in and zoom-out work. (Increasing the number of categories for an unsupervised method carries much less risk than doing the same with a supervised method.)
:::

## Measuring the "Meaning" of Rationality

::: {.highlight-last}

::: {.smaller-text}
::: {.callout-tip .nonincremental}
### Embeddings
Embeddings models represent words or sentences as vectors in a multidimensional space that captures their meaning and usage.
:::
::: 

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="65%"}
::: {.center-content .smaller-text}
![](../images/fake_semantic_space_words_in_2D.png){width=75%}
:::
::: 

::: {.column width="35%" .highlight-last}
::: {.callout-note .fragment appearance="minimal"}
- Our goal:  
    1. Use *contextual* embeddings (rather than *static*) to vectorize texts related to rationality
    2. Group these vectors into clusters (different meanings of rationality)
:::
:::

::::

::: 

:::{.notes}
- *Embeddings* model: models trained to represent words or sentences as vectors in a multidimensional space.
  - Trained on large text corpora to predict the context of words, or missing words, or consecutive sentences.
- The position of words in this space reflects their meaning and usage. Greater proximity = greater semantic similarity.
- Measured by cosine similarity: a value between -1 and 1 indicating how closely two vectors point in the same direction.
- Static embeddings: each word has a unique representation, regardless of context.
- Contextual embeddings: the representation of a word or sentence depends on the context in which it appears, capturing finer semantic nuances. Allows polysemy to be taken into account. That's the basic technique behind LLMs.
:::

## Our data 

::: {.highlight-last .smaller-text}
::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" .fragment}
- We build a corpus of 800k+ full-text documents.
- Three sources: economic journals in JSTOR, completed by Elsevier + ISTEX.
- We kept for the analysis: 
  - Research articles (excluding book reviews, editorials, etc.);
  - Articles published between 1900 and 2009;
  - Articles in English.
- Resulting in a corpus of 258k+ research articles.
::: 

::: {.callout-caution appearance="minimal" .fragment}
Not in the presentation but we also retrieve citation data to run bibliometric analyses. 
::: 

::: {.callout-important appearance="minimal" .fragment}
Clear room for improvement: english bias, exclusion of books, etc. 
::: 

::: 

## Sentence Vectors

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
We use *sentence-BERT*, a language model that maps **sentences** to vectors optimised for semantic similarity tasks.
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| output: false
source(here::here("scripts", "paths_and_packages.R"))
data_tbl <- arrow::read_feather(here::here(
  data_path,
  "top_sentences_to_fake_sentence.feather"
))



make_tbl <- function(years, new_year = NULL) {
  tbl <- data_tbl |>
    filter(rank < 4, year %in% years) |>
    mutate(similarity = round(similarity_fake, 3)) |>
    select(year, sentence, similarity) |>
    gt::gt() |>
    gt::tab_options(table.font.size = 15)
  if (!is.null(new_year)) {
    tbl <- tbl |>
      gt::tab_style(
        style = gt::cell_text(weight = "bold"),
        locations = gt::cells_body(rows = year == new_year)
      )
  }
  tbl
}
```

## Measuring Polysemy & Semantic Evolution

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}

:::{.fragment}
::: {.center-content .smaller-text}
![@giulianelliAnalysing2020, "Analysing Lexical Semantic Change with Contextualised Word Representations"](../images/giulianelli_example.png){width=60%}
:::
::: 

::: 

::: {.column width="40%" .highlight-last}

::: {.callout-note .fragment appearance="minimal"}
- Extract sentences using a particular word (e.g. "coach")
- Vectorise these sentences 
- Cluster these vectors
::: 

::: {.callout-important .fragment appearance="minimal"}
- Two issues: 
  - Only explicit uses of the word are captured
  - Can't handle bias of corpus growing over time 
::: 

::: 

::::

:::{.notes}
- Embeddings useful for measuring polysemy, but how exactly? A paper that interested us, particularly for its temporal visualisations.
- Appearance and prevalence of senses over time.
- How it works: here we get the impression that genuine senses are being identified, but what we see are reworked examples of those senses. The underlying result consists of clusters of sentences containing the term. Each cluster is interpreted as a different sense. That is the idea.
- In their paper, they apply this to a very large vocabulary. For us, only two words. Possibility of zooming in much more and being more fine-grained in the analysis. Desire to truly take the historical dimension into account (corpus much larger in recent years, which risks overshadowing older periods).
:::

## Empirical Strategy

::: {.highlight-last .tiny-text}
1. Vectorise the 61M sentences in the corpus using sentence-BERT.
1. Compute the "representative vectors":
    1. Select all vectors of sentences containing "rational" or "rationality";
    1. Each year, compute the moving average of these vectors;
    1. This average vector is the "representative vector", $RV$: it captures the meaning of rationality in a given year.

2. Extract sentences closest to this vector. For each year:
    1. Compute the cosine similarity between $RV$ and the sentence vectors for this year;
    2. Select the top 1% most similar sentences.

3. Clustering: 
    1. Group sentences by decade;
    1. Group clusters across decades to identify "meta-clusters" that persist over time.
:::



## Visualising clusters as a network

::: {layout-ncol=2}

![Static](../images/backbone_communities_network.png){width=90% fig-align="center"}

![Dynamic](../images/temporal_network_plot.png){width=90% fig-align="center"}

::: 

:::{.notes}
- Unsatisfactory pairwise comparison of clusters, well illustrated by the uselessness of the "flows", led us back to networks.
- Forget the colours. Each point is a cluster in a decade. Links represent similarity. Pruning method to keep only the statistically most significant links.
- Broader view rather than pairwise. See how nodes group together, which ones are close. Using the network to create meta-clusters.
- Provides a centre/periphery perspective, and also shows which clusters are most connected to each other, and which ones form less uniform groupings.
- What is the main problem here? Loss of the historical dimension. How to reintroduce history without losing too much information.
- Finding how to position clusters on the vertical axis: hierarchical clustering to group together the closest meta-clusters.
:::

## But What Do These Clusters Correspond To?

::: {.highlight-last .very-small-text}
- We need to _select_ and _hierarchise_ the most relevant information to characterise clusters and make them interpretable. 
  - Development of a set of complementary indicators
    - Most frequent words
    - Representative sentences
    - Representative articles
    - Cited references
- How to share this information with readers and reviewers ?
  - Production of long HTML reports in appendix but hardly readable and replicable by readers.
  - Development of an interactive application for exploring results
:::


## {background-iframe="https://019adac8-81d4-aa0e-808c-08861c261fd2.share.connect.posit.cloud/" background-interactive="true"}

## Some results from our analysis

:::{.highlight-last .small-text}
- Our analysis recovers well early-20th-century debates among institutionalist economists, notably around the concept of “pecuniary” institutions.
- A social dimension of rationality emerges as early as the 1930s, with the promotion of "rationalizing" economic processes and institutions.
- The theory of the firm plays an important role in critiques of what came to be viewed as the standard conception of rationality.
- Debates on individual rationality and choice theory remain relatively limited in the 1960s and 1970s, before the rise of behavioural economics.
:::
